newsitem.title: UK: Britain strikes sceptical note on EU integration.
newsitem.headline: Britain strikes sceptical note on EU integration.

text.p: Britain's Conservative prime minister and two of his top ministers warned on Monday of the dangers of a headlong rush by European Union states towards closer integration.
Prime Minister John Major and finance minister Kenneth Clarke expressed scepticism about whether the planned launch of a single European currency in less than 23 months time was sensible or feasible.
Meanwhile, Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind appealed in a speech in Stockholm for a slowing-down of EU institutional changes which Britain fears may be leading towards a federal super-state.
"I do not believe this pace of change can be sustained," he told Sweden's Institute of International Affairs.
The French newspaper Le Figaro quoted Major in an interview as saying that if the single currency was launched as planned on January 1, 1999, "it's clear that we (Britain) will not be part of it".

But Major's office rushed out a denial of these remarks, saying he had merely ruled out British participation if there was no "reliable and sustainable convergence" of the economies of those countries which did go ahead.

Clarke, however, said in a broadcast interview that he believed the EU would put back the launch date for the new Euro within months, and called for countries who back the idea to temper their enthusiasm for it with common sense.

"Nobody should contemplate EMU (economic and monetary union) unless countries are genuinely convergent and are going to stay convergent in the economic conditions that are essential to get the best out of a single currency," he said.
By contrast, Robin Cook, foreign affairs spokesman of the opposition Labour Party, on Monday stressed the disadvantages to Britain if it stayed outside a successful single currency area.
He told BBC radio in an interview that Britain needed to achieve genuine economic convergence with other EU states if it was to join a single currency in 1999.
But he added: "In the longer run...a country that stays out of the European single currency could face penalties.
"For instance inward investment decisions taken in Tokyo, taken in Dallas, are more likely to go within the single core currency than into an offshore currency."

Rifkind, in the first in a series of speeches in European capitals to explain Britain's view of the EU, said changes were being made too fast -- from the 1986 Single European Act to the 1992 Maastricht Treaty on closer integration.

"Britain's vision for Europe is not one of rolling integration toward a single federal destiny. It is about finding the right balance between supernationalism and inter-governmentalism," he said. Rifkind said "supranational integration" was needed in areas such as the EU single market, and cooperation made sense in, for example, fighting drug trafficking.
But in areas which "go to the heart of the relationship between the citizen and the state", the EU should have no role.

"It may be that in some countries people are ready to have a European Police Force patrolling their streets, to be subject to arrest and detention by European justice authorities...But in Britain they are not," Rifkind said.
